correctness.rationale: For m,n>=3 the tensor graph has diameter 2, and every edge can be extended to a 2-edge geodesic, so any maximal geodesic uses exactly 3 vertices, bounding the number by floor(mn/3). Each digit in all six full displayed brick arrays occurs at 3 distinct cells inducing exactly 2 graph edges, so gives a maximal geodesic. Every integer >=3 splits into blocks of width 3 with at most one block of width 4 or 5. All blocks touching dimension 3 cover all vertices, and at most one 4/5-by-4/5 block leaves 1 or 2, exactly area modulo 3, proving the lower bound uniformly. Standalone validator checks six certificates, 2304 board instances and independent small-board enumeration; finite checks are not used as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The assessed contribution is an exact all-dimensions near-perfect induced-P3 geodesic tiling of K_m×K_n for m,n>=3. The fully read foundational geodesic packing source proves a general upper bound and handles Cartesian rook graphs, not the tensor complement. The fully read direct-product EOP source handles induced matchings/edge-open packing, which are different invariants and do not imply a vertex-disjoint P3-tiling. Four targeted published-record queries, extensive public-literature search variants and prior scientific comparisons found no stronger covering statement. Older induced-P3 tiling/factor terminology remains a residual overlap risk, so this assessment is not a universal novelty certification.
residual_risks: Graph-factorization or induced-P3 near-factor literature may express an equivalent result without using geodesic packing nomenclature and may be poorly indexed.
Search results and accessible full texts cannot establish universal independence from all historic or unpublished work.

value.rationale: Geodesic packing is a natural established graph invariant. The theorem gives a sharp exact formula and a constructive near-perfect induced-path tiling for every member of the unrestricted two-parameter tensor-product family, a distinct graph operation from the rook graph treated in the foundational paper. The six residue bricks solve genuine congruence obstacles, providing a reusable decomposition algorithm rather than a single small-case table. It neither relies on arbitrary artificial slices nor simply recomputes a known graph table.
